title: Is the Uncanny Valley Real?
summary: Josh and Chuck explore the Uncanny Valley hypothesis, starting with Masahiro Mori's 1970 Japanese essay "Bukimi no Tani Gen" (translated as Uncanny Valley in 2005 and officially in 2012), and its graph of human likeness versus affinity. They cover the translation debate (bukimi closer to "eerie"), the lack of scientific rigor (undefined variables, Texas sharpshooter fallacy), research by Talia Wheatley, Angela Tinwell, Karl MacDorman, and David Hanson, and the role of eyes and facial features. They discuss Hollywood's CGI misfires (Tin Toy's Billy, Final Fantasy, The Polar Express, Beowulf, Tintin, Rogue One's Peter Cushing, Mars Needs Moms), robots like Geminoid F, Ellie, and Casper, and Ernst Jentsch's 1906 essay on the uncanny and Freud. They then cover the psychology of "the creeps," including Dickens' use of the phrase, theories like pathogen avoidance, mortality salience, and category ambiguity (David Livingstone Smith), and a Knox College survey on creepiness. The episode ends with listener mail about the Choctaw Nation's famine donation to Ireland.

segments.title: Opening banter and introduction to Mori's 1970 essay
segments.summary: Hosts open with banter about robot dancing, then introduce Masahiro Mori's 1970 essay on bukimi (the uncanny valley) and note its late translation and the naming debate.

segments.title: The uncanny valley graph and its examples
segments.summary: Mori's graph plots human likeness against affinity. Examples run from industrial robots and stuffed animals to C-3PO, Pixar-style exaggerated characters, and the dip into the valley where corpses and zombies sit, with separate animate and inanimate lines.

segments.title: Precursors and the open casket example
segments.summary: Ernst Jentsch's earlier idea of the uncanny (heimlich/unheimlich) is introduced, along with the sense that seeing a lifelike object move is creepy, illustrated with baby dolls and open-casket funerals.

segments.title: Why the uncanny valley is hard to study
segments.summary: The hosts explain the research problems: subjective dependent variable, undefined human likeness independent variable, no mathematical model, and the Texas sharpshooter fallacy.

segments.title: Break
segments.summary: Short break before resuming the discussion.

segments.title: Cross-cultural research, eyes, and evolution
segments.summary: Talia Wheatley's Dartmouth work found the effect across cultures, including Cambodian tribes, with the eyes as a key cue. Angela Tinwell links upper facial features to the effect, and Karl MacDorman links personality traits such as religiosity, neuroticism, and animal-reminder sensitivity to it. A Princeton study with monkeys is also mentioned.

segments.title: Skeptics, robot design, and real-world robots
segments.summary: David Hanson's survey found no one was disturbed by his robots, while the hosts caution about cherry-picked data. Mori's view on prosthetic hands is discussed, and robot designers such as Hiroshi Ishiguro (Geminoid F, Ellie) and the Casper robot for children with autism are described.

segments.title: Hollywood CGI failures and successes
segments.summary: Pixar's Tin Toy and Billy, Final Fantasy, The Polar Express, Beowulf, The Adventures of Tintin, Rogue One's Peter Cushing, and Mars Needs Moms are discussed as examples of the uncanny valley in film. Pixar's shift to exaggerated features is presented as a lesson learned.

segments.title: Mori's take on designing around the valley and the Asimo robot
segments.summary: Mori advised designers to avoid chasing realism and instead use stylized forms, such as sanded wood hands. His student created Asimo, which is cute and non-human.

segments.title: The psychology of creepiness
segments.summary: The hosts discuss the origin of 'the creeps' (Dickens), Jentsch's essay on the uncanny, and theories of creepiness including pathogen avoidance, mimicry, violation of expectation, mortality salience, and pareidolia-like dehumanization. A Knox College survey on creepy traits and occupations is described.

segments.title: Threat ambiguity and category ambiguity theories
segments.summary: The hosts cover threat ambiguity theory and David Livingstone Smith's category ambiguity theory, which ties creepiness to uncertainty about a thing's species essence, illustrated with wax figures. They conclude that the theory fits the uncanny valley and wrap up.

segments.title: Listener mail: Choctaw Nation and Irish famine
segments.summary: A listener describes the Choctaw Nation's 1845 donation to Irish famine relief, the Cork sculpture, the 1990 Famine Walk, and the 1992 Trail of Tears walk that raised money for famine relief in Africa.

segments.title: Sign-off
segments.summary: Hosts thank listeners and sign off with contact information.
